titre_chapitre: Production Cycles, Product Types, and Bills of Materials (BOM)

questions.enonce: What are the three distinct cycles that make up the generic model of production processes?
options: The production cycle, the commercial cycle, and the financial cycle.
The purchasing cycle, the manufacturing cycle, and the distribution cycle.
The short-term, medium-term, and long-term cycles.
The planning cycle, the scheduling cycle, and the quality cycle.
questions.explication: The generic model relies on three fundamental cycles to take into account: the production cycle, the commercial cycle, and the financial cycle[span_0](start_span)[span_0](end_span)[span_1](start_span)[span_1](end_span).

questions.enonce: Why is the commercial cycle considered the most critical from the customer's perspective?
options: Because it completely excludes manufacturing lead times.
Because it is the only cycle known to the customer, measured between their order and delivery, and serves as a basis for comparison with competitors.
Because it directly determines the salary of workshop operators.
Because it guarantees the total absence of intermediate inventories.
questions.explication: The commercial cycle is the only one known to the customer (from the moment of order to receipt of the product), making it a key competitive advantage to optimize[span_2](start_span)[span_2](end_span)[span_3](start_span)[span_3](end_span).

questions.enonce: What is the main distinction between a standard product and a specific product?
options: A standard product is manufactured for a single customer, whereas a specific product is intended for a broad audience.
A standard product is purchased by a large number of customers without distinction, whereas a specific product is made according to the wishes of a particular customer.
There is no technical difference between the two.
A standard product necessarily incorporates intangible services.
questions.explication: A standard product is acquired by many customers without modification (e.g., a laundry pack), while a specific product is designed according to the requirements of a particular customer (e.g., a custom-made suit)[span_4](start_span)[span_4](end_span)[span_5](start_span)[span_5](end_span).

questions.enonce: How does product complexity (measured by the number of components) impact the probability of manufacturing according to the course?
options: It increases the probability of overall success.
It has no effect on production risks.
It multiplies unavailability risks, causing the overall probability of having all components gathered at the same time to drop.
It eliminates the need to use purchasing BOMs.
questions.explication: Complexity introduces risks: for example, with 3,000 components each having an excellent availability of 99.99%, the overall probability of having all components available is only 74%[span_6](start_span)[span_6](end_span)[span_7](start_span)[span_7](end_span).

questions.enonce: What rule applies to negative coefficients (resulting from an extraction operation, such as digging) when calculating the purchasing BOM?
options: They must be subtracted from the purchased quantities.
They must not be taken into account (no negative coefficient) when calculating the overall quantities to be purchased.
They are multiplied by the scrap rate.
They completely replace the financial cycle.
questions.explication: Negative coefficients should not be used in calculating final purchasing quantities, because just because a quantity was extracted does not mean it did not have to be purchased initially[span_8](start_span)[span_8](end_span)[span_9](start_span)[span_9](end_span).
